cAMP signaling pathways and downstream effectors

cAMP signaling pathways and downstream effectors. cAMP is generated through two mechanistically distinct pathways: (i) G-protein-dependent manner, the dissociation of the Gαs from the dimer Gβγ subunits, leading to the activation of the adenylyl cyclases (ACs), which form the cAMP by catalyzing the conversion of ATP into cAMP (tmAC-derived cAMP; global signaling at the plasma membrane); and (ii) GPCR-independent manner, bicarbonate (HCO3-) and calcium ions activate the soluble adenylyl cyclase (sAC) to synthesize cAMP(sAC-derived cAMP; localized microdomain signaling within intracellular compartments including the cytoplasm, nucleus, and mitochondria). These sAC-generated cAMP microdomains enable compartmentalized signaling that is functionally independent from plasma membrane–associated tmACs. However, cAMP is degraded to adenosine 5-monophosphate (5’AMP) via phosphodiesterases (PDEs). The cAMP regulates three different downstream protein effectors: the protein ion channel, associating in the regulation of the heart rate, olfactory transduction, and calcium signaling pathways; holoenzyme PKA (two C subunits, two R subunits), C subunits phosphorylate transcription factor (CREB) responsible in regulating the CRE genes with the association of CBP and CRTCs coactivators, and, the phosphorylation of specific targets by PKA particular, due to the A kinase anchor proteins (AKAPs), anchoring the PKA in localized sites; EPAC/Rap pathway activate different signaling, implicating in many biological and pathophysiological processes via Rap1/2 activation, through releasing the Rap1 and Rap2 (Ras family proteins) the GDP and binding to GTP to activate the Rap1/2. Furthermore, sAC-derived cAMP microdomains in the nucleus and mitochondria contribute to the regulation of metabolic rewiring and apoptosis
